loop:0.t: The R L Loop. Learning by doing: try something, see what happens, adjust.

loop:1.t: Words you’ll need. Agent: the learner. It makes the choices. Environment: everything outside the agent: the world it acts in. Action: one choice the agent makes, like “move left”. Reward: a number the world hands back. High means good, low means bad.

loop:2.t: Two players. Reinforcement learning has two sides. The agent is the learner. The environment is the world around it. They take turns, again and again. In the animation: The pink dot is the agent’s action travelling to the world. The teal dot coming back carries the new state, with a gold reward beside it. One lap is one time step.

loop:3.t: One turn of the loop. The agent looks at the situation, called the state. It picks an action. The world reacts: it moves to a new state and hands back a reward. In the animation: One turn, slowed down: the agent sees its square, picks “move right”, the world moves it and hands back a reward. The reward is 0 until the robot reaches the flag.

loop:4.t: Think of a puppy. You say “sit”. The puppy tries something. If it sits, it gets a treat. Over many tries, it learns which action earns the treat. In the animation: The puppy tries a random trick every couple of seconds. The teal bars show how likely each trick is. Every treat makes the rewarded trick more likely next time. Try it: Tap to give a treat whenever the puppy does a trick you like. For example: Puppy = agent. You and the room = environment. Treat = reward.

loop:5.t: No answer key. Nobody tells the agent the right move. It only gets a score. That is the big difference from normal machine learning, where every example comes with the correct answer.

loop:6.t: Rewards can be late. Often the score only arrives at the very end. The agent must work out which earlier choices deserved the credit. For example: A chess bot learns it lost only after 60 moves. Which move was the mistake?

loop:7.t: More examples. A game AI presses buttons and gets points. A robot moves its motors and gets closer to the cup. An app picks a video and you keep watching.

loop:8.t: The goal. Collect as much reward as possible over the long run, not just on the next turn. Everything else in R L builds on this loop.

loop:9.t: In a nutshell. Agent acts, environment answers with a new state and a reward. No correct answers given, only scores. Goal: the most total reward over time.

returns:0.t: Rewards & Returns. Why the agent cares about the total, not just the next snack.

returns:1.t: Words you’ll need. Reward: the score for one single step. Return: all the rewards from now on, added up. Episode: one full attempt, from start to finish, like one game.

returns:2.t: Reward: instant feedback. After every step the agent gets one number. Positive is good, negative is bad, zero means nothing special happened.

returns:3.t: Return: the running total. The return, written G, adds up every reward from now until the end. The bars show rewards piling up into one total. In the animation: Each column is one time step. Green bars are positive rewards, red are negative. The gold bar on the right is the return G, the running total, growing as the robot moves on.

returns:4.t: Small now, big later. A step that costs a little now can lead to a big win later. So the agent should judge a choice by the return, not by the next reward. In the animation: Two plans, one day at a time. The boxes are daily rewards and the box on the right is the running total, the return. Plan B starts worse but ends far ahead. For example: Studying tonight costs fun (minus 1). Passing the exam next week is worth plus 10.

returns:5.t: A maze example. Each step in a maze costs minus 1, and reaching the exit gives plus 10. The shortest path has the highest return, because it wastes the fewest steps. In the animation: Two robots walk to the door: teal takes the short route, gold the long one. Each step adds the step cost, the door adds plus 10. The numbers on the right are each route’s return. Try it: Drag the step cost to 0 and both routes tie.

returns:6.t: Tasks that end. Some tasks have a natural finish: a game, a maze, a race. These are called episodic. Each attempt is one episode.

returns:7.t: Tasks that never end. Others just keep going, like a thermostat or a stock trader. These are continuing tasks. Their return could grow forever, which the next reel fixes.

returns:8.t: The big bet. R L assumes any goal can be written as “get the largest total reward”. Not everyone agrees, but it has worked surprisingly well.

returns:9.t: In a nutshell. Reward: the number for one step. Return: the sum of rewards from now on. Judge choices by their long-run return.

discount:0.t: The Discount Factor gamma. A reward tomorrow is worth a bit less than a reward today.

discount:1.t: Words you’ll need. Return: all the rewards from now on, added up. Discount factor gamma: gamma, a number between 0 and 1 that shrinks future rewards. Horizon: how far into the future the agent effectively cares.

discount:2.t: Money today versus later. Would you take 100 rupees now or 100 rupees in a year? Most people pick now. R L agents are built to feel the same way.

discount:3.t: Shrink the future. Each step into the future, a reward is multiplied by gamma once more. One step away: times gamma. Two steps: times gamma twice. The bars shrink as they get further. In the animation: Every bar is the same +1 reward, placed further in the future to the right. Its height is what it’s worth today. Watch gamma change: small gamma makes far rewards shrink fast.

discount:4.t: A worked example. Say gamma is 0.9 and a reward of 10 is three steps away. It counts as 10 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9, which is about 7.3. In the animation: Each bar is a reward of 10 placed further in the future. Its height is what it is worth today: 10 times gamma, once for every step of waiting. The gold bar shows the sum. Try it: Drag gamma and watch far-away rewards shrink or grow.

discount:5.t: Why bother?. Three reasons. It keeps never-ending sums from blowing up. It makes the agent prefer faster wins. And the far future is uncertain anyway.

discount:6.t: Small gamma: impatient. With gamma close to 0, only the next reward or two matter. The agent grabs quick wins and ignores long plans. In the animation: The robot can grab a candy worth 1 now, or walk 6 more steps for a gift worth 10. The box shows what each is worth today with this gamma. The robot picks the bigger number. Try it: Push gamma above 0.68 and the robot switches to the big gift. For example: With gamma = 0.5, a reward 10 steps away counts for about one thousandth.

discount:7.t: gamma close to 1: patient. With gamma near 1, far-away rewards still count. The agent plans ahead, but learning is slower and noisier.

discount:8.t: Rule of thumb. The agent looks roughly 1 divided by (1 minus gamma) steps ahead. With gamma = 0.99, that is about 100 steps. In the animation: The teal curve shows how much a reward counts depending on how many steps away it is. The gold line marks one over one minus gamma: roughly how far ahead the agent really looks. Try it: Slide gamma towards 0.99 and watch how far the agent looks.

discount:9.t: In a nutshell. Each step away multiplies a reward by gamma. Small gamma = impatient, gamma near 1 = patient. Looks about 1/(1 minus gamma) steps ahead.

mdp:0.t: Markov Decision Process. The board game that almost every R L problem is written as.

mdp:1.t: Words you’ll need. State: a snapshot of the situation right now. Transition: the move from one state to the next after an action. Probability: how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (always).

mdp:2.t: A rulebook for the world. A Markov Decision Process, or M D P, is just a careful description of the world the agent lives in. Most R L problems are written this way.

mdp:3.t: The ingredients. A list of states. A list of actions. Rules for where each action can take you. A reward for each move. And the discount gamma.

mdp:4.t: A tiny M D P. A race car can be Cool, Warm or Overheated. Driving fast earns plus 2 but might overheat it, which costs minus 10. Driving slow is safe but earns less. In the animation: Three circles are the car’s states. Grey arrows show where it can go next, labelled with probabilities. The gold token hops randomly each step, and each landing shows its reward.

mdp:5.t: Luck is allowed. The same action can lead to different results. Driving fast while Warm might keep you Warm, or might overheat you. The chances are fixed, but the outcome is random. In the animation: The robot is on ice and always tries to move right. Usually it does, but sometimes it slips up or down. The bars count what actually happened; they drift towards 80, 10 and 10 percent. Try it: Tap to make the robot step right. Count how often it slips.

mdp:6.t: The Markov property. The current state tells you everything you need about the future. How you got here does not matter. In the animation: Two views of a Pong game. On the left, one still picture: you cannot tell which way the gold ball moves. On the right, the faded trail of recent frames shows its direction. For example: Chess: the board is enough. You don’t need the move history to pick the next move.

mdp:7.t: When it fails. Sometimes the state hides things. One frozen frame of a ball game doesn’t show which way the ball is moving. Then the snapshot is not enough.

mdp:8.t: Why it matters. If the state is a full summary, the agent can decide using only “where am I now?”. That makes learning far simpler.

mdp:9.t: In a nutshell. M D P = states, actions, transition rules, rewards, gamma. Outcomes can be random. Markov: the present state is all you need.

policy:0.t: Policies. The agent’s rulebook: in this situation, do that.

policy:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy pi: pi, the agent’s strategy: what to do in each state. Deterministic: always the same choice. Stochastic: involves chance, like rolling a die.

policy:2.t: What is a policy?. A policy is the agent’s behaviour written down: for every state, which action to take. The arrows show one policy for a small grid world. In the animation: A small maze: green flag is +1, fire is minus 1, the black square is a wall. Arrows show the policy, what to do in each square, and the robot follows them to the flag. In the coloured version, brighter means more valuable.

policy:3.t: Like a cheat sheet. Imagine a card that says “if you see this, do that” for every situation. Following the card is following the policy. In the animation: The robot walks the grid. At each square it looks up its row in the cheat sheet on the right, highlighted in pink, and does what it says. That table is the policy. For example: Red light: stop. Green light: go. Yellow: slow down.

policy:4.t: Deterministic policies. A deterministic policy always picks the same action in the same state. It is simple to write down and easy to predict, which is great for a robot arm on a factory line.

policy:5.t: Stochastic policies. Give each action a chance instead. For example: go left 70 percent of the time, right 30 percent. Handy for trying new things. In the animation: Each square has four arrows. A thicker arrow means a higher chance of taking that move. The robot rolls the dice at every step, so with more randomness its walks wander more. Try it: Slide randomness to 0 for a deterministic policy, up for chaos. For example: In rock-paper-scissors, the best policy is one third each. Being predictable loses.

policy:6.t: Learning = better policies. Almost every R L method is a recipe for taking the current policy and turning it into a better one, step by step.

policy:7.t: The best policy. The optimal policy, written pi star, earns at least as much return as any other policy, from every state.

policy:8.t: In a nutshell. Policy pi: what to do in each state. Deterministic (fixed) or stochastic (chances). R L searches for the best policy pi star.

values:0.t: Value Functions. How good is it to be here? How good is this move?

values:1.t: Words you’ll need. Value: how much return you expect from here, on average. Expected: the average result if you could try many times. V and Q: V scores a state. Q scores a state plus an action.

values:2.t: A score for every place. A value function gives each state a score: how much total reward you can expect from there. Bright squares are worth more. In the animation: A small maze: green flag is +1, fire is minus 1, the black square is a wall. Arrows show the policy, what to do in each square, and the robot follows them to the flag. In the coloured version, brighter means more valuable.

values:3.t: State value V of s. V of s answers one question: “If I start in this state and keep following my policy, how much return do I collect on average?” One number per state. In the animation: Every square shows its value: the reward you can expect from there, with gamma 0.9. Bright squares are close to the flag. The pink robot walks from the chosen square to show why. Try it: Tap any square to see its value and the walk behind it.

values:4.t: Action value Q of s, a. Q of s, a answers: “If I take this action here first, and follow my policy afterwards, how much return do I get?” In the animation: The big square on the right is the pink square from the small map, split into four triangles, one per move. Each shows that move’s Q value. The gold outline marks the best move. For example: Standing at a fork in the road: Q tells you how good “left” is and how good “right” is.

values:5.t: Why Q is handy. If you know Q, acting well is easy. In each state, pick the action with the biggest Q. No map of the world needed.

values:6.t: Chess intuition. Strong chess players have a feel for value. They don’t calculate every future move. They glance at a position and sense whether it is good or bad. For example: “This position is winning for white” is a high V. “Taking the queen here is great” is a high Q.

values:7.t: Values depend on the player. The same chess position is worth more to a grandmaster than to a beginner. So values are always measured for a particular policy.

values:8.t: In a nutshell. V of s: expected return from a state. Q of s, a: expected return of an action in a state. Pick the action with the biggest Q.

bellman:0.t: The Bellman Equation. Value of here = reward now + discounted value of next.

bellman:1.t: Words you’ll need. Value: how much total reward you expect from a state, on average. Recursive: defined in terms of itself, one step at a time. Backup: passing value from a future state back to the current one. Next state: where you land after one action.

bellman:2.t: One step is enough. You don’t need to imagine the whole future. The value of here equals the reward for one step, plus the value of wherever you land. In the animation: A one-step look-ahead tree. Bottom circles are the values of places you might land. They flow up into each action’s score Q, in gold, and the best action becomes the top value.

bellman:3.t: In words. Value of here = reward now + gamma times value of next. If the next state is random, average over where you might land.

bellman:4.t: A small worked example. One step from the goal, the reward is 1, so that square is worth 1. With gamma = 0.9, the square before it is worth 0.9, the one before that 0.81, and so on. In the animation: A corridor ending at a flag. All values start at 0. Each sweep applies the Bellman rule to every square, so the value spreads one square left each time: 1, then 0.9, then 0.81. Try it: Tap to run one sweep and watch the value travel left.

bellman:5.t: Like a rumour spreading. Value starts at the treasure and spreads outward, square by square, getting a little weaker each step. In the animation: A gridworld solved by repeated sweeps. Colours are values: bright squares are worth a lot. Watch the brightness spread outwards from the flag, one step per sweep. For example: Ask a friend how far the beach is. They ask their neighbour, who has been there. The answer flows back.

bellman:6.t: For the best policy. To find the best value, use the best next action each time: take the max over actions instead of following a fixed policy.

bellman:7.t: Everywhere in R L. Value iteration, T D learning, Q-learning and D Q N are all different ways of making this one equation come true.

bellman:8.t: In a nutshell. Value = reward now + gamma times value of next state. Value flows backwards from the future. The base of most R L algorithms.

explore:0.t: Exploration versus Exploitation. Order your favourite dish, or try something new?

explore:1.t: Words you’ll need. Exploit: use what you already know works. Explore: try something else to learn more. Greedy: always picking what looks best right now.

explore:2.t: The dilemma. Every choice is a trade-off. Exploit your current best option, or explore something new that might turn out even better.

explore:3.t: Your favourite restaurant. Always ordering your usual dish is exploiting. Trying the new place down the road is exploring. It might be awful, or it might become your new favourite. In the animation: Four restaurants; question marks mean you have never tried that one. You eat at your favourite for five days, then risk a new place and find a 5-star one. The teal bar is total happiness.

explore:4.t: Greedy gets stuck. A purely greedy agent picks whatever looks best so far. One lucky early win and it may stick with a mediocre option forever. In the animation: Four slot machines. Teal bars are the agent’s guesses, gold dashes the true payouts. Pure greedy always pulls the arm that looks best and can get stuck on a worse one.

explore:5.t: Too much exploring. The opposite mistake: always trying new things means you rarely enjoy the good ones you found. Endless experimenting wastes reward.

explore:6.t: The balance. Explore a lot at first, when you know very little. Then explore less as you become more sure, and spend more of your time on the options you know are good. In the animation: Average payout per pull as the agent learns. The teal curve uses your epsilon, the grey dashed one never explores, and the gold line is the best arm. A little exploring wins; a lot wastes pulls. Try it: Try epsilon = 0, 0.1 and 0.5. Which ends highest? For example: New in town: try many cafés. After a year: mostly go to the best two.

explore:7.t: Real life. Music apps mix your favourites with new songs. Doctors give the best-known drug, but also test new ones in trials.

explore:8.t: Strategies ahead. Random tries (epsilon-greedy), optimism (U C B), random guesses from beliefs (Thompson sampling), and curiosity. Each has its own reel.

explore:9.t: In a nutshell. Exploit the known best versus explore the unknown. Pure greedy can lock in a bad choice. Explore less as you grow more certain.

bandits:0.t: Multi-Armed Bandits. R L with one room and a row of slot machines.

bandits:1.t: Words you’ll need. Arm: one option you can pick, like one slot machine. Payout: the reward an arm gives when pulled. Regret: how much you lost by not always picking the best arm.

bandits:2.t: The setup. A row of slot machines. Each one pays out differently on average, but you don’t know which is best. Every turn you pull one. Win as much as you can. In the animation: Three slot machines with hidden payout rates. Each pull either pays a coin or not. Teal bars are your average so far. After 15 pulls the gold numbers reveal the true rates. Try it: Tap a machine to pull it. Can you find the best one?

bandits:3.t: Why “bandit”?. Old slot machines had one lever, an “arm”, and took your money, like a bandit. Many machines means a multi-armed bandit.

bandits:4.t: Watch it learn. Each bar is one machine’s estimated payout. Pulling an arm updates its estimate. The question is always which arm to pull next. In the animation: Four slot machines. Teal bars are the agent’s guesses, gold dashes the true payouts. Mostly it pulls the best-looking arm, but one time in ten it tries a random one.

bandits:5.t: Only one situation. Pulling an arm doesn’t change the world. There are no states to plan over. That makes bandits the purest test of exploring versus exploiting.

bandits:6.t: Regret. Compare your winnings to someone who always pulled the best arm. The gap is your regret. Good methods keep regret growing slowly. In the animation: Regret piles up every time the agent pulls a worse arm. Red never explores and keeps losing, teal explores at random, gold uses U C B. A flatter curve means the agent has found the best arm.

bandits:7.t: Real uses. Websites test two designs and send more visitors to the better one. Ad systems and news apps work the same way. For example: Show headline A or headline B? Each click is a reward.

bandits:8.t: Adding context. Contextual bandits also look at who the user is before choosing. They sit halfway between bandits and full R L.

bandits:9.t: In a nutshell. Several arms, unknown payouts, pick one each turn. Measure performance by regret. Used in A/B tests, ads, recommendations.

epsgreedy:0.t: epsilon-Greedy. Mostly do the best thing, occasionally roll the dice.

epsgreedy:1.t: Words you’ll need. epsilon (epsilon): a small number, like 0.1, that sets how often you act randomly. Estimate: your current best guess of how good an option is. Decay: shrinking a number gradually over time.

epsgreedy:2.t: The rule. Most of the time, pick the option that looks best. But with a small chance epsilon, pick a completely random option instead. In the animation: Four slot machines. Teal bars are the agent’s guesses, gold dashes the true payouts. Mostly it pulls the best-looking arm, but one time in ten it tries a random one.

epsgreedy:3.t: In numbers. With epsilon = 0.1, you pick the best-looking option 9 times out of 10. One time in 10, you roll the dice and pick any option at random, even a bad-looking one. In the animation: Before every pull the agent rolls a random number, the pink arrow. If it lands in the gold zone, smaller than epsilon, it picks any machine at random. Otherwise it picks the best one so far. Try it: Raise epsilon and the gold explore zone grows.

epsgreedy:4.t: Why it works. Because every option keeps getting tried now and then, a wrong first impression eventually gets corrected. For example: A café you rated badly after one off day gets a second chance, and you discover it’s great.

epsgreedy:5.t: Shrink epsilon over time. Start with lots of random tries, then lower epsilon as your estimates firm up. Learn first, then cash in. In the animation: The gold curve is epsilon shrinking over time. Each dot below is one pull: gold dots explore, teal dots exploit. Early on there are many gold dots, later almost none. For example: The Atari-playing D Q N started fully random and slowly dropped to 10 percent random.

epsgreedy:6.t: The weakness. It explores blindly. It wastes pulls on options already known to be terrible, just as often as on promising ones.

epsgreedy:7.t: Still a favourite. It takes one line of code and works surprisingly well, so it is often the first thing people try.

epsgreedy:8.t: In a nutshell. Random action with chance epsilon, otherwise the best-looking one. Simple and surprisingly strong. Explores blindly; usually shrink epsilon over time.

ucb:0.t: Upper Confidence Bound. Be optimistic about what you haven’t tried much.

ucb:1.t: Words you’ll need. Estimate: your current best guess of how good an option is. Uncertainty: how unsure you are about an estimate. Bonus: extra points added to make an option more tempting. Optimism: assuming the best about what you don’t know yet.

ucb:2.t: Benefit of the doubt. If you’ve barely tried something, it might be great. U C B gives such options extra credit so they get checked.

ucb:3.t: The score. Each arm gets a score: its estimate plus an uncertainty bonus. Always pull the arm with the highest score. The tall caps on the bars are the bonuses. In the animation: Four slot machines. Teal bars are guesses, gold dashes the true payouts. The gold whisker on top is an uncertainty bonus: rarely-tried arms get a bigger one, so they get tried.

ucb:4.t: The bonus shrinks. Every time you pull an arm, you learn more about it, so its bonus gets smaller. Rarely-tried arms keep a big bonus until checked. In the animation: Each arm’s score is a teal estimate plus a gold bonus for uncertainty. The arm with the highest total gets pulled. Watch the gold part shrink on arms that are pulled often. Try it: Tap an arm to pull it and watch its gold bonus shrink.

ucb:5.t: Smarter than random. Unlike epsilon-greedy, U C B stops trying arms it is confident are bad. It spends its exploring where it can still learn something. In the animation: Total regret over time for three strategies. Gold is U C B: it explores only where it is unsure, so its regret flattens out sooner than random epsilon-greedy in teal or greedy in red. For example: A new café gets a visit. After three bad coffees, you stop going.

ucb:6.t: A famous descendant. The same idea, used for choosing moves in a game tree, is called UCT. It helped AlphaGo decide which moves to think about.

ucb:7.t: Where it shines. U C B needs no random dice and no tuning of epsilon. It works best when payouts stay steady over time. If the best arm keeps changing, its old confidence can mislead it. For example: Steady: which button colour gets more clicks. Changing: which news story is hot today.

ucb:8.t: In a nutshell. Score = estimate + uncertainty bonus. The bonus shrinks the more you try an arm. Also guides game-tree search (UCT).

thompson:0.t: Thompson Sampling. Act on a random guess drawn from your beliefs.

thompson:1.t: Words you’ll need. Belief: your sense of how likely each possible payout is. Distribution: a spread of possible values with their chances. Sample: one random draw from a distribution.

thompson:2.t: Beliefs, not single numbers. Instead of one guess per arm, keep a range of what its payout could be. A wide range means unsure. A narrow range means confident. In the animation: Four slot machines. Each purple shape is the agent’s belief about that arm’s payout, wide when unsure. Each pull it samples from every belief and plays the winner. Beliefs sharpen over time.

thompson:3.t: The rule. Each turn, draw one random guess from every arm’s range. Pull the arm whose guess came out highest. Then update that arm’s range. In the animation: Purple hills are the agent’s beliefs about each arm’s payout rate. Each round it draws one random guess from every hill, the pink pins, pulls the arm with the highest guess and updates that hill.

thompson:4.t: Built-in balance. Unsure arms produce wild guesses, so now and then they win the draw: that is exploring. Clearly good arms win most draws: that is exploiting.

thompson:5.t: An example. An online shop has two product photos. Photo A: 50 clicks out of 1000 views. Photo B: 3 clicks out of 4 views. For example: B looks amazing but is based on almost nothing. Its wide range means it still gets shown sometimes, until the shop knows.

thompson:6.t: Ranges get narrower. Every pull adds evidence, so ranges tighten. Over time the agent naturally stops exploring arms it has figured out. In the animation: The purple hill is the belief about one arm’s payout rate, between 0 and 1. Every win pushes it right, every loss left, and more results make it narrower. The gold line is the likely range. Try it: Tap or to add results and watch the hill narrow.

thompson:7.t: Old but strong. The idea dates from 1933, and it is still one of the best methods for many bandit problems today.

thompson:8.t: In a nutshell. Keep a belief range for each arm. Draw a guess from each, pull the highest. Exploration comes naturally from uncertainty.

valueiter:0.t: Value Iteration. Know the rules? Spread value outward from the goal, step by step.

valueiter:1.t: Words you’ll need. State: where the agent is right now, like one square of a maze. Value: how much total reward you can expect from a state onward. Model: the rules of the world: where each move takes you and what it pays. Greedy: always picking whatever looks best right now.

valueiter:2.t: The problem. Sometimes you already know the rules of the world, like a maze on paper. Then you don’t need trial and error. You can sit down and compute the best plan. For example: A delivery robot with a full floor map of the warehouse.

valueiter:3.t: The core idea. Think of the goal as a lamp. Its light spreads to the squares next to it, then to their neighbours, and so on. Each square learns how close it is to the light. In the animation: A maze with a goal flag. Every 1.3 seconds one sweep updates all squares: the numbers spread out from the goal, fading with distance. At the end, arrows show the best move. Try it: Tap any square to move the goal. Drag gamma to change how fast values fade.

valueiter:4.t: One sweep. Visit every state. For each, look at every move and ask: reward now, plus the value of where I land. Keep the best of those as the new value. In the animation: Each square shows its value V. Every sweep, each square looks one step ahead and updates. Brightness spreads out from the green flag, and at the end arrows show the best move.

valueiter:5.t: A tiny example. The goal pays 10, and future reward is shrunk by 0.9 per step. After sweep 1, squares beside the goal are worth 10. After sweep 2, squares two steps away are worth 9. In the animation: A row of squares with the goal on the right. Each sweep, one more square learns its value: the goal’s 10 shrinks by gamma for every step of distance. Teal bars show the values. Try it: Drag gamma: at 0.9 you get 10, 9, 8.1 … as in the text. For example: Three steps away: 0.9 times 9 = 8.1. The numbers fade with distance.

valueiter:6.t: When to stop. Keep sweeping until the values barely change. Then the plan is easy: from any square, move to the neighbour with the highest value. That is the greedy policy. In the animation: A small maze: green flag is +1, fire is minus 1, the black square is a wall. Arrows show the policy, what to do in each square, and the robot follows them to the flag. In the coloured version, brighter means more valuable.

valueiter:7.t: Where it’s used. Small planning problems with known rules: robot paths on small maps, stock and inventory decisions, simple games. For example: How many units to reorder each week, given known demand odds.

valueiter:8.t: The catch. It needs the full rules and a pass over every state. Fine for a grid of 100 squares, hopeless for Go, which has more board positions than atoms in the universe.

valueiter:9.t: In a nutshell. Needs the rules of the world. Sweep all states: best reward plus next value. Stop when values settle, then act greedily.

policyiter:0.t: Policy Iteration. Judge your plan, fix it, repeat, until nothing changes.

policyiter:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy: the agent’s rulebook: in this situation, do that. Value: how much total reward you can expect from a state onward. Greedy: always picking whatever looks best right now.

policyiter:2.t: The idea. Start with any plan, even a silly one. Then repeat two steps: judge how good the plan is, and fix it wherever a better move exists.

policyiter:3.t: Step 1: evaluate. Work out the value of every state if you follow the current policy. This tells you how good each place is under your plan. In the animation: Two phases take turns. Teal: evaluate the current arrows, so the colours show how good each square is. Pink: improve, where changed arrows light up. It stops when nothing changes.

policyiter:4.t: Step 2: improve. In each state, look one move ahead using those values. If some move looks better than what the policy does, switch to it. In the animation: Arrows are the current plan in each square. Evaluate fills in how much each square is worth under that plan, improve flips arrows (gold) that point the wrong way. Repeat until nothing flips. Try it: Tap the picture to step through evaluate and improve yourself. For example: Your route to work goes via the highway. Values show the side road is faster from one junction, so you change that one turn.

policyiter:5.t: It only gets better. Each fix makes the plan at least as good as before. There are only so many possible plans, so it must stop, and when it stops, the plan is the best one. In the animation: The same plan improving round by round. Values (numbers) only go up between rounds, and once no arrow flips, the plan is the best possible.

policyiter:6.t: Few rounds. It usually finishes in just a handful of rounds. The catch is that each evaluation step can be slow, because it scores every state.

policyiter:7.t: The big template. Almost all R L is a loose version of this, called generalised policy iteration: estimate values a little, improve the policy a little, repeat. For example: Actor-critic methods do exactly this, but with learning instead of exact sums.

policyiter:8.t: In a nutshell. Alternate: evaluate the plan, then improve it. Each round is at least as good as the last. Ends at the best plan. Template for most R L methods.

mc:0.t: Monte Carlo Learning. Play to the end, then learn from what really happened.

mc:1.t: Words you’ll need. Episode: one full run of a task from start to finish, like one game. Return: the total reward collected from a moment until the episode ends. Value: the return you expect on average from a state. Variance: how much results jump around from one try to the next.

mc:2.t: The problem. Often we don’t know the rules of the world. We can’t compute values on paper. But we can play, and watch what happens.

mc:3.t: The core idea. Like judging a restaurant by eating there many times. Play whole episodes, write down the return that followed each state, and average them.

mc:4.t: How it works. After an episode ends, go back through every state you visited. Add the total reward that came after it to that state’s list, and update its average. In the animation: The robot plays a whole episode, leaving a gold trail. Only when it ends does it update: every square it visited moves toward the real total it got. Colours show the learned values.

mc:5.t: A worked example. From one state, three games give returns of 10, 4 and 7. The value estimate is their average, 7. A fourth game scoring 9 nudges it to 7.5. In the animation: Each blue dot is the total reward of one finished game from the same state. The pink line is their running average, the value estimate. It wobbles at first, then settles near the gold true value. Try it: Tap to play another game and watch the average move. For example: Blackjack: value of holding 18 = average result over thousands of hands from 18.

mc:6.t: Honest but noisy. It uses real outcomes, so it never fools itself with guesses. But one very lucky or unlucky game swings the average a lot: high variance. In the animation: Each blue dot is the total reward of one finished game from the same state. The pink line is their running average, the value estimate. It wobbles at first, then settles near the gold true value. Try it: Drag luck up: games vary more and the average takes longer to settle.

mc:7.t: The catch. It can only learn when an episode finishes. For a task that never ends, like running a power grid, there is nothing to average. For example: Next idea: learn after every step instead. That’s T D learning.

mc:8.t: In a nutshell. Learn from complete episodes. Value = average of the returns seen. Honest, but noisy. Must wait for the episode to end.

td:0.t: Temporal-Difference Learning. Learn a guess from a slightly better guess, every single step.

td:1.t: Words you’ll need. Value: how much total reward you expect from a state onward. Estimate: your current best guess, which gets corrected over time. Bootstrapping: improving a guess using another guess, instead of waiting for the truth.

td:2.t: The problem. Monte Carlo waits until the end of a game to learn anything. That is slow, and impossible if the task never ends. Can we learn after every step?

td:3.t: The core idea. Guess your commute takes 30 minutes. Halfway, you hit traffic and now expect 40. You update right away, without waiting to arrive. That is T D learning. In the animation: A drive home with checkpoints. Each box is the guess for the total trip time made at that point. The T D row corrects the previous guess at every checkpoint; the Monte Carlo row waits until you arrive.

td:4.t: How it works. After one step, build a better guess: the reward you just got plus your estimate for the next state. Move the old estimate a little toward it. In the animation: The robot updates after every single step. The gold curved arrow shows each square borrowing a guess from the square it just stepped into. Values spread back from the flag.

td:5.t: The surprise signal. The gap between the better guess and the old one is the T D error: was that better or worse than I expected? All learning is driven by this surprise. In the animation: Blue dots are noisy targets, one per step. The pink line is the value guess: each step it moves a fraction alpha of the T D error (the green or red bar) toward the target. Try it: Drag alpha: big steps chase every surprise, small steps crawl but stay calm. For example: Expected 5, got reward 1 and the next state is worth 6: new guess 7. Surprise is +2, so raise the estimate a bit.

td:6.t: T D versus Monte Carlo. T D learns online and is less noisy. The price: its targets lean on its own guesses, so early mistakes can mislead it for a while.

td:7.t: Brains do it too. Dopamine neurons in the brain fire like a T D error. They react to unexpected reward, not to reward itself, and go quiet when a promised reward fails to come.

td:8.t: What it leads to. Apply T D to actions instead of states and you get two famous algorithms: SARSA and Q-learning.

td:9.t: In a nutshell. Update after every step, not at the end. Target: reward plus next-state guess. T D error = surprise signal. Less noisy than Monte Carlo, a bit biased.

qlearning:0.t: Q-Learning. Learn the value of every move, even while acting randomly.

qlearning:1.t: Words you’ll need. Q-value: how good it is to take a given action in a given state, then play well. Learning rate: how big a step you take toward each new target, often called alpha. T D target: reward now plus a guess about the future. Explore: try something new to find out how good it is.

qlearning:2.t: The goal. Instead of scoring places, score moves. For every state and action, learn one number: how good is it to do this here, then play as well as possible?

qlearning:3.t: The update. After each step, form a target: reward now plus the best Q-value in the next state. Move the old Q-value a small step toward it. In the animation: Each square is split into four triangles, one per move: up, right, down, left. A triangle brightens when that move turns out good. Watch good moves light up a path to the flag.

qlearning:4.t: A worked example. Q for “right” here is 2. You get reward 1, and the best move in the new square is worth 5. Target: 1 + 0.9 times 5 = 5.5. With a learning rate of 0.1, Q becomes 2.35. In the animation: One Q-learning update, slowly. The robot moves right and gets 1. The best value in the next square is 5. Target 5.5, error 3.5, and the old 2 moves a tenth of the way: 2.35.

qlearning:5.t: Assume the best. The target uses the best next move, even if you actually explore with a random one. So it learns the values of playing perfectly, while you play sloppily. In the animation: Four slot machines. Teal bars are the agent’s guesses, gold dashes the true payouts. Mostly it pulls the best-looking arm, but one time in ten it tries a random one.

qlearning:6.t: A table of numbers. Classic Q-learning keeps a table with one number per state and action. Great for small worlds. In the animation: A robot explores a short corridor. Below is its Q-table: one box per square and move. After every step the gold box updates, and good values spread backwards from the goal. For example: The Taxi puzzle has 500 states and 6 actions: a 3000-cell table, solved in seconds.

qlearning:7.t: The leap. Replace the table with a neural network and you get D Q N, which learned to play Atari games straight from the screen pixels in 2015.

qlearning:8.t: In a nutshell. One value per state and action. Target: reward plus best next Q. Learns optimal play while exploring. Table version leads to D Q N.

sarsa:0.t: SARSA. Learn the value of what you’ll actually do next.

sarsa:1.t: Words you’ll need. Q-value: how good it is to take a given action in a given state. Explore: sometimes trying a random move to learn more. On-policy: learning about the same behaviour you are actually using.

sarsa:2.t: The name. SARSA is spelled by the five things it uses: State, Action, Reward, next State, next Action, the one you really chose.

sarsa:3.t: The update. Target: reward now plus the Q-value of the next action you actually take, not the best one. Then move the old Q-value a small step toward it.

sarsa:4.t: Why that matters. If you sometimes take random moves, SARSA’s values include those mistakes. It learns how good things are for you, slips and all. In the animation: Both robots explore with random steps. Pink, Q-learning, learned the route along the cliff edge, so random steps make it fall. Teal, SARSA, counted its own randomness and walks further from the edge. Try it: Drag epsilon up: the pink robot falls more and SARSA’s route moves away from the edge.

sarsa:5.t: Cliff walking. A path runs along a cliff edge. Q-learning learns the shortest path, right on the edge. SARSA knows it sometimes stumbles, so it learns a safer detour. In the animation: The red strip is a cliff worth minus 100. The pink dot, Q-learning, walks the risky edge path and sometimes falls when it explores. The teal dot, SARSA, takes the safer route along the top.

sarsa:6.t: An everyday version. A learner driver keeps extra distance from parked cars, because they know they sometimes swerve. That is SARSA thinking. For example: Expert drivers can cut it close. Learners shouldn’t, yet.

sarsa:7.t: When to choose it. Use SARSA when mistakes during learning are costly, like a real robot near stairs. It trades a little speed for safer behaviour while learning. In the animation: Count the falls: with random steps, the edge route of Q-learning (pink) costs many falls during learning, while SARSA (teal) stays safe. Try it: Set epsilon to 0: with no randomness both learn the same short route.

sarsa:8.t: In a nutshell. Target uses the action you really take next. On-policy: values include your exploration. Learns safer paths near danger.

onoff:0.t: On-Policy versus Off-Policy. Learn only from your own behaviour, or from anyone’s?

onoff:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy: the agent’s rulebook: in this situation, do that. Behaviour policy: the rulebook actually used to act and collect data. Target policy: the rulebook you are trying to learn and improve.

onoff:2.t: Two roles. Every learner has one policy that acts and gathers experience, and one policy being learned. The big question: are they the same?

onoff:3.t: On-policy. They are the same. You learn about exactly what you do, exploration included. SARSA and P P O work this way. In the animation: The red strip is a cliff worth minus 100. The pink dot, Q-learning, walks the risky edge path and sometimes falls when it explores. The teal dot, SARSA, takes the safer route along the top.

onoff:4.t: Off-policy. They differ. You act one way, maybe randomly, but learn the best possible policy. Q-learning, D Q N and sack work this way. In the animation: Two learners. The blue trail is how each one actually behaves; the arrows are the plan it is learning. On the left they are the same plan. On the right, random wandering still teaches the best plan. For example: Learning to drive well by watching dashcam videos of other people.

onoff:5.t: Why off-policy is powerful. You can reuse old experience, learn from humans or other agents, and explore freely without hurting what you learn. In the animation: Old experiences are stored and pulled out again at random. Only off-policy learners can safely learn from these memories of past behaviour.

onoff:6.t: Why it is harder. The data comes from a different policy than the one you’re learning, so it can mislead. Corrections and stabilising tricks are needed. For example: Watching a cautious driver tells you little about what happens at high speed.

onoff:7.t: Rule of thumb. On-policy: simpler and steadier, but needs fresh data constantly. Off-policy: more data-efficient, but trickier to keep stable.

onoff:8.t: In a nutshell. Acting policy versus learned policy. On-policy: the same one (SARSA, P P O). Off-policy: different, reuses data (Q-learning, D Q N).

traces:0.t: Eligibility Traces & T D(lambda). Give credit to recent steps, fading into the past.

traces:1.t: Words you’ll need. Credit assignment: figuring out which earlier choices caused a later reward. Trace: a fading mark left on each state you recently visited. T D(0): T D learning that looks just one step ahead.

traces:2.t: The problem. A reward arrives. Which earlier steps deserve the credit? One-step T D credits only the last step. Monte Carlo credits all of them equally.

traces:3.t: The core idea. Like footprints in snow that slowly fill in. Each state you visit gets a mark, a trace, that fades a little every step. In the animation: Footprints behind the robot fade step by step. When the reward arrives, fresher footprints get more of the credit (green).

traces:4.t: How it works. When a reward or surprise arrives, every state gets updated in proportion to its trace. Recent states change a lot, old ones barely. In the animation: As the robot walks, squares it passed glow gold. That glow is the eligibility trace, and it fades with each step. When the reward arrives, recently glowing squares get the most credit.

traces:5.t: The dial lambda. lambda (lambda), a number from 0 to 1, sets how slowly traces fade. 0 means one-step T D. 1 means Monte Carlo. Values in between often learn fastest. In the animation: The robot walks right. Every square it passes gets a purple trace bar that shrinks by lambda each step. When the reward arrives, each square gets credit in proportion to its trace (green). Try it: Drag lambda to 0: only the last square gets credit. At 1, all squares share it. For example: lambda = 0.9: a state visited 5 steps ago still gets about 0.6 of the credit, before discounting.

traces:6.t: A famous success. T D-Gammon, built by Gerald Tesauro in 1992, used T D(lambda) and self-play to reach world-class backgammon.

traces:7.t: An everyday version. After winning a game, you remember the last few moves that sealed it more vividly than your opening. That fading memory is an eligibility trace.

traces:8.t: In a nutshell. Traces mark recently visited states. A reward updates states by their trace. lambda slides between one-step T D and Monte Carlo.

funcapprox:0.t: Function Approximation. Too many states for a table? Learn a function that generalises.

funcapprox:1.t: Words you’ll need. Function: a recipe that turns inputs into an output number. Features: useful measurements describing a state, like distance or speed. Neural network: a flexible function with many adjustable knobs, tuned from data. Generalise: use what you learned on some cases to handle new similar ones.

funcapprox:2.t: Tables don’t scale. A value table needs one entry per state. Camera images, robot joints, Go boards: there are far too many states, and most are never seen twice.

funcapprox:3.t: The core idea. Instead of memorising every state, learn a function that predicts value from the state’s description. Learning about one state then teaches you about similar ones. In the animation: Gold dots are states the agent has seen. Left, a table only knows boxes it has visited, and the rest are question marks. Right, a teal curve fills the gaps with a smooth guess.

funcapprox:4.t: An everyday version. You don’t memorise the price of every house. You learn a rule of thumb: bigger and closer to the city means more expensive. That rule works on houses you’ve never seen. In the animation: Blue dots are houses we have seen, the pink line is the learned rule. The gold is a house never seen: the rule still predicts its price. Add points and the rule refits. Try it: Tap the chart to add a house; the line refits and the ? price changes.

funcapprox:5.t: Features. The function reads features of the state. They can be hand-made, like distance to goal, or learned automatically by a deep network from raw pixels. For example: Cart-pole: cart position, cart speed, pole angle, pole spin.

funcapprox:6.t: How it learns. Each time you get a better target value, nudge the function’s knobs so its prediction for that state moves a little toward the target.

funcapprox:7.t: The catch. Changing the function for one state also changes many others. Mixed with guess-based targets and off-policy data, learning can blow up: the deadly triad. In the animation: The pink curve is the learned value across many states. Training it toward one gold target also drags the nearby part of the curve: grey dashed shows how it was before. Try it: Tap anywhere to set a target and see neighbours move too. For example: Fixing one prediction shifts its neighbours, which shifts the targets, which shifts everything again.

funcapprox:8.t: In a nutshell. Replace tables with a learned function. Generalises to states never seen. Features describe states. Beware the deadly triad.

dqn:0.t: Deep Q-Network (D Q N). Q-learning plus a neural network: superhuman Atari from pixels.

dqn:1.t: Words you’ll need. Q-value: how good it is to take an action in a state, then play well. Neural network: a flexible function with many adjustable knobs, tuned from data. Pixels: the tiny coloured dots that make up a screen image.

dqn:2.t: The problem. Q-learning needs a table, one number per state and action. An Atari screen has astronomically many possible images. No table could ever hold them.

dqn:3.t: The core idea. Let a neural network read the game screen and output one Q-value per joystick action. Then pick the action with the highest score. In the animation: A tiny Pong-like screen goes into a neural network, the blue dots. Out come three bars, the Q-values for left, stay and right. The gold bar is the biggest, and that move is taken.

dqn:4.t: The 2015 milestone. DeepMind used one algorithm, with the same settings, on 49 Atari games, learning only from pixels and the score. It beat human level on many of them.

dqn:5.t: Seeing motion. One frame can’t show which way the ball moves. So D Q N feeds the last 4 frames together, letting the network see motion. In the animation: A ball in a brick game. On the left, one still frame: you can’t tell where the ball is going. On the right, the last four frames overlap as a fading trail, so the direction is obvious. For example: In Breakout, a single frame can’t tell you whether the ball is rising or falling.

dqn:6.t: Why naive training fails. Back-to-back frames are nearly identical, so the network overfits to the moment. And its targets shift every time it learns: unstable. In the animation: Tiles are experiences coloured by moment. Training on the latest few in order means a batch of nearly identical moments; a random batch from memory is varied.

dqn:7.t: Two key tricks. Experience replay shuffles old memories to break the patterns. A target network holds the targets still for a while. Each gets its own reel.

dqn:8.t: In a nutshell. Neural net outputs a Q-value per action. Learned 49 Atari games from pixels (2015). Stacks 4 frames to see motion. Needs replay and a target network.

replay:0.t: Experience Replay. Store experiences, then learn from random old memories.

replay:1.t: Words you’ll need. Transition: one step of experience: state, action, reward, next state. Buffer: a big memory that stores past transitions. Minibatch: a small random handful of examples used for one training update. Correlated: samples so alike that they teach the same thing again and again.

replay:2.t: The problem. Learning from steps in the order they happen is like studying only the last page you read. Consecutive frames are nearly identical, and old lessons get forgotten.

replay:3.t: The core idea. Keep a diary of experiences. Every step, write down what you saw, did, got, and where you ended up. In the animation: Coloured boxes are stored experiences in the buffer. The pink arrow writes new ones, overwriting the oldest. Each time, a few random boxes, outlined gold, are sent to the learner.

replay:4.t: How it works. Store each transition in a big buffer, like the last 1 million steps. To train, pull out a random minibatch of, say, 32, and learn from those.

replay:5.t: Why it helps. Random picks break the correlation between samples. And each experience gets reused many times, so you need far fewer steps in the world. In the animation: Each tile is one stored experience, coloured by when it happened. A batch taken in order is all one colour, nearly identical. A random batch from the buffer mixes many moments. For example: A rare crash in a driving game gets replayed many times, instead of seen once and forgotten.

replay:6.t: Prioritised replay. An upgrade: replay surprising transitions, the ones with a big T D error, more often than boring ones. In the animation: Ten stored memories. Red bars show how surprising each was, teal bars count how often it was replayed. More priority means surprising ones get picked far more. Try it: Drag priority to 0: every memory is replayed equally often. For example: Like re-reading the exam questions you got wrong rather than the easy ones.

replay:7.t: The limit. Old memories came from an older version of the agent. That’s fine for off-policy methods like D Q N, but on-policy methods like P P O can’t use a big replay buffer.

replay:8.t: In a nutshell. Store transitions in a big buffer. Train on random minibatches. Breaks correlation and reuses data. Works for off-policy methods.

targetnet:0.t: Target Networks. Stop chasing your own tail: freeze the target for a while.

targetnet:1.t: Words you’ll need. T D target: reward now plus a guess about the future, used as the answer to learn toward. Weights: the adjustable numbers inside a neural network. Copy: a second network with the same weights as the first.

targetnet:2.t: The problem. In D Q N, the target the network learns toward is computed by the same network. Every update moves the target too, so you chase your own tail.

targetnet:3.t: An everyday version. Imagine aiming at a dartboard that jumps every time you throw. Hitting a board that stays put for a minute is much easier.

targetnet:4.t: The fix. Keep a second, frozen copy of the network just for computing targets. Train the main network toward those steady targets. In the animation: The gold line is the target, frozen for a while and then copied, where dashed lines say copy. The pink line is the online network chasing it. A still target makes the chase calmer.

targetnet:5.t: Refreshing the copy. Every N steps, say every 10,000, copy the main network’s weights into the frozen one. Then the targets hold still again until the next copy. In the animation: Pink is the network’s prediction, gold the target it trains toward. With no frozen copy the target moves with every update, so pink overshoots and wobbles. A frozen copy is slower but steady. Try it: Drag N up from 1: the gold target becomes stairs and pink stops wobbling.

targetnet:6.t: Soft updates. Another option: every step, blend the copy slowly toward the main network, like 99.5% old, 0.5% new. D D P G and sack use this. In the animation: Gold is a slowly blended copy of the network that provides targets, pink is the network. A small blend keeps the target smooth but slower to catch up. Try it: Drag τ: tiny values give a smooth target, large ones a jumpy one. For example: The target drifts smoothly instead of jumping.

targetnet:7.t: Why it works. It turns one endless chase into a series of short, fixed learning problems. Training becomes much more stable.

targetnet:8.t: In a nutshell. Targets come from a lagging copy. Copy every N steps, or blend slowly. Much steadier training.

doubledqn:0.t: Double D Q N. Taking a max over noisy guesses is too optimistic.

doubledqn:1.t: Words you’ll need. Q-value: a guess of the total future reward for taking an action in a situation. D Q N: a neural network that learns Q-values, famous for playing Atari games. Target network: a slowly updated copy of the network, used to compute learning targets. Bias: a mistake that leans the same way every time, not random noise.

doubledqn:2.t: The problem. D Q N learns by asking: what is the best next action worth? It answers by taking the max over its own Q-value guesses. But those guesses are noisy, and the max loves noise. In the animation: Every action is truly worth zero, but each guess has random noise. The gold bar is the biggest guess. On the right, pink averages the max over many tries and teal the double estimate. Try it: Raise the noise or add actions and watch the pink average climb.

doubledqn:3.t: Why the max is optimistic. Imagine ten actions that are all truly worth 0. Your guesses are 0 plus random errors. The biggest guess is almost always above zero, so you overestimate by pure luck. In the animation: All six actions are truly worth zero. Left: picking the biggest noisy guess, in gold, keeps looking positive, shown by the pink average line. Right: Double scores the pick with fresh numbers, and the average stays near zero. For example: Ten people guess the weight of a cow. The highest guess is almost always too high.

doubledqn:4.t: It snowballs. That too-high number becomes the learning target for the previous step, which feeds the step before it. The overestimation spreads backwards and can make the agent chase actions that only look good. In the animation: Five states in a row, each truly worth zero. Each round, every box copies its target from the box to its right. Pink max targets creep upward and spread backwards; teal double targets stay near zero.

doubledqn:5.t: The fix in plain words. Split the job in two. One network chooses which next action looks best. A different network scores that choice. Their errors don’t line up, so the lucky spike gets cancelled out.

doubledqn:6.t: A tiny example. The online network says action B looks best, at 5.2. The target network scores B at only 3.1. Double D Q N learns from 3.1, not 5.2, giving a calmer, more honest target. For example: Asking one friend to pick the restaurant and another friend to rate it.

doubledqn:7.t: Almost free. D Q N already keeps two networks, the online one and the target copy. So Double D Q N is basically a one-line change. It came from Hado van Hasselt’s Double Q-learning, scaled up to deep networks in 2015.

doubledqn:8.t: Same idea, everywhere. Continuous-control methods like T D 3 and sack keep two critics and trust the lower of their two guesses. Different trick, same goal: stop the max from fooling itself. For example: Getting two quotes for a repair and planning around the cheaper, more cautious one.

doubledqn:9.t: In a nutshell. A max over noisy guesses is too optimistic. Errors spread backwards through targets. Choose with one net, score with the other. T D 3 and sack use the min of two critics.

pg:0.t: Policy Gradient Methods. Skip the values: directly tweak the policy to win more.

pg:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy: the agent’s rule for picking an action in each situation. Parameters: the adjustable numbers inside a model, like knobs. Gradient: the direction to turn the knobs to make a number go up fastest. Return: the total reward collected from now until the end.

pg:2.t: A different route. Many methods first learn how good each action is, then pick the best. Policy gradient methods skip that middle step and adjust the policy itself to collect more reward.

pg:3.t: The policy as a dial board. Make the policy a neural network with parameters that outputs a probability for each action. Learning means nudging those numbers so good actions get likelier. In the animation: Each column is one action. The purple dial is a policy parameter, and the bar below is that action’s probability. Turning one dial up makes its action likelier and the others a bit less likely. Try it: Tap a column to turn its dial up; tap reset to start over.

pg:4.t: The core intuition. Try something. If things went better than usual, make those actions more likely. If worse, make them less likely. Repeat thousands of times. In the animation: Four bars are the probabilities of four moves. Each try picks one: a reward makes its bar grow, a bad outcome makes it shrink. Over time the bar for right, the good move, takes over. For example: A basketball player who drifts toward shots that tend to go in.

pg:5.t: A tiny example. The policy picks left 50% and right 50%. Going right earns a big reward. After a small update it might pick right 55% of the time. Many small steps add up. In the animation: The top bar splits the policy between left and right. Every second it tries one, sees a noisy reward, and nudges that action’s odds up or down. The teal line tracks the chance of picking right. Try it: Drag the step size: big steps learn fast but jump around.

pg:6.t: Why bother?. It handles continuous actions naturally: just output a number, like a steering angle. It can also learn deliberately random policies, which matter in games against opponents. For example: A robot arm choosing a torque of 0.37. There is no table of every possible torque.

pg:7.t: The catch. The signal is noisy. One lucky episode can push the policy the wrong way, so it needs many samples. A lot of later ideas, like baselines and critics, exist to calm that noise.

pg:8.t: In a nutshell. Adjust the policy directly, not values. Good outcomes make those actions likelier. Natural for continuous actions. Noisy, so needs many samples.

reinforce:0.t: REINFORCE. The simplest policy gradient: weight actions by the episode’s return.

reinforce:1.t: Words you’ll need. Episode: one complete run, from start to finish, like one game. Return: the total reward collected from a step until the episode ends. Monte Carlo: learning from the real outcomes of complete episodes. Variance: how much results jump around from one try to the next.

reinforce:2.t: The idea in one line. Play a whole episode. Then, for every action you took, make it more likely in proportion to the return that came after it. That’s the whole algorithm.

reinforce:3.t: Step by step. One: play an episode with the current policy. Two: for each step, add up the rewards that followed. Three: nudge each action’s probability up by an amount scaled by that total. In the animation: The robot plays an episode. At the end, every move it made gets judged by the final score: big green arrows mean make these more likely, thin red ones mean less likely.

reinforce:4.t: A tiny example. An episode has three moves and ends with a reward of 10. Each move gets credit 10, so all three become a bit more likely. An episode ending in minus 5 pushes its moves down. In the animation: Three moves play out, then the episode’s final reward appears on the right. Every move gets that same total as its credit. A plus 10 pushes all three up, a minus 5 pushes all three down.

reinforce:5.t: Honest but noisy. It uses real outcomes, so on average it points the right way. But one episode’s luck colours every action in it, so the updates have high variance. In the animation: The gold dashed arrow is the truly best direction to change the policy. Each pink arrow is one update estimated from real episodes. With one episode they swing wildly; averaging more steadies them. Try it: Average more episodes and watch the pink arrow settle. For example: A winning chess game makes every move in it likelier, even the blunder the opponent failed to punish.

reinforce:6.t: Where it came from. Ronald Williams introduced REINFORCE in 1992. It is still used today, for example to fine-tune text generators against a reward score.

reinforce:7.t: Taming the noise. Two fixes lead to the next reels. Subtract a baseline, so only better-than-usual returns push actions up. Or replace the real return with a learned critic, giving actor-critic.

reinforce:8.t: In a nutshell. Play an episode, then credit every action. Credit = the return that followed. Unbiased but very noisy. Baselines and critics reduce the noise.

baseline:0.t: Baselines & Advantage. Not “was it good?” but “was it better than usual?”

baseline:1.t: Words you’ll need. Return: the total reward collected from a step until the episode ends. Value V of s: the return you expect on average from a situation. Baseline: a reference score you compare each outcome against. Advantage: how much better an action did than the usual outcome.

baseline:2.t: The problem. Suppose every episode scores around plus 100. Plain REINFORCE then pushes every action up, good or bad. The useful signal, which actions did slightly better, is buried. In the animation: Eight episodes. Teal ones used action A, which is slightly better; purple ones used B. Each arrow is how hard that action is pushed: its return minus the baseline. At baseline 0 everything goes up. Try it: Drag the baseline to about 100: only A keeps getting pushed up.

baseline:3.t: Compare to normal. Instead of asking “was this good?”, ask “was this better than usual?” Subtract a baseline from each return, and only the difference drives learning. In the animation: Each arrow is the push given to one action. Left: all returns are big, so every arrow points up. Right: the average is subtracted first, so better than usual goes up and worse goes down. For example: Grading on a curve: 75 is great if the class average is 60, and poor if it is 90.

baseline:4.t: A tiny example. From some situation you normally get 100. This time you got 104, so the action gets plus 4: a gentle push up. Another time you got 95, so minus 5: a gentle push down.

baseline:5.t: The best baseline. A natural baseline is V of s, the return you usually get from that situation. A second network can learn it alongside the policy.

baseline:6.t: Advantage. Return minus baseline has a name: the advantage. It says how much better this action did than the policy’s average from here. Positive means do it more, negative means less. In the animation: Blue bars show how much each action is worth here. The gold dashed line is the usual value of the situation. Each arrow is the advantage: green above the line means better than usual, red means worse.

baseline:7.t: No free lunch? Almost. As long as the baseline doesn’t depend on which action you took, it doesn’t change the average direction of learning. It only removes noise, so learning gets much faster.

baseline:8.t: In a nutshell. Raw returns push every action up. Subtract a baseline: better than usual?. Advantage = return minus expected value. Same direction, far less noise.

actorcritic:0.t: Actor-Critic. One network acts, another grades every move.

actorcritic:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy: the agent’s rule for picking an action in each situation. Value function: a learned guess of how much reward lies ahead from a situation. T D error delta: the surprise: how much better or worse a step went than predicted. Online learning: updating after every step instead of waiting for the episode to end.

actorcritic:2.t: Two roles. The actor is the policy: it chooses what to do. The critic is a value function: it judges how good the situation is. They learn together. In the animation: Three boxes: the actor picks an action, the environment gives a reward, and the critic compares it with its guess. Green means better than expected, red worse, and the actor adjusts.

actorcritic:3.t: An analogy. An athlete and a coach. The athlete tries a move, the coach immediately says “better than I expected” or “worse”. The athlete adjusts, and the coach keeps refining their judgement too.

actorcritic:4.t: How one step works. The actor acts and gets a reward. The critic compares its prediction with reward plus its guess for the next state. The gap is the T D error delta (delta). Positive delta: do that more. In the animation: One step in four stages. The critic guesses this state is worth 10. The actor acts and gets a reward. The gap is the T D error delta. Then the critic’s guess and the actor’s odds both shift. For example: Critic expected 10. You got reward 2 and the next state looks worth 9. That is 11, so delta = plus 1.

actorcritic:5.t: Why it helps. REINFORCE waits for the episode to end and is very noisy. Actor-critic learns every step and uses the critic’s steadier estimate, so it’s usually faster and calmer.

actorcritic:6.t: The trade-off. The critic is only a guess. If it’s wrong, it can steer the actor wrong. That adds a bit of bias in exchange for much less noise, a trade most modern methods happily make. In the animation: Each dot is one estimate of how good an action was; the gold centre is the truth. Pink real returns land around the centre but scatter. Teal critic guesses cluster tightly, off to one side.

actorcritic:7.t: A big family. A2C, A3C, P P O, D D P G, T D 3 and sack are all actor-critic methods. Most of today’s deep R L, from game agents to robot controllers, works this way.

actorcritic:8.t: In a nutshell. Actor picks actions, critic judges them. T D error tells the actor better or worse. Learns every step, less noisy. Basis of P P O, sack, T D 3 and more.

gae:0.t: n-step Returns & G A E. How far should you look before trusting the critic’s guess?

gae:1.t: Words you’ll need. Critic: a learned guess of how much reward lies ahead from a situation. Bootstrapping: using your own guess of the future instead of waiting to see it. Bias: a mistake that leans the same way every time. Variance: how much results jump around from one try to the next.

gae:2.t: The question. To judge an action, you can wait and add up real rewards, or stop early and trust the critic’s guess for the rest. How many real steps should you look at first?

gae:3.t: n-step returns. Add up the next n real rewards, then plug in the critic’s estimate for everything after. With n equal to 1 you lean almost fully on the critic; with large n, mostly on reality. In the animation: The circles are the rewards that really came. The agent counts the first n in teal, then the purple block is the critic’s guess for everything after. The meters show the trade you make. Try it: Slide n from 1 to 8 and compare the estimate with the truth. For example: n = 3: reward 1, reward 0, reward 2, then the critic says 7 is left. Total about 10.

gae:4.t: The trade-off. Small n: steady, low variance, but wrong if the critic is wrong, which is bias. Large n: right on average, but noisy because many random rewards pile up. In the animation: Each dot is one estimate and the gold centre is the truth. Pink: long n-step returns, centred but scattered. Teal: one-step returns that lean on the critic, tight but off-centre.

gae:5.t: G A E: mix them all. Generalised Advantage Estimation doesn’t pick one n. It blends all of them, giving nearer ones more weight. A single knob, lambda (lambda) between 0 and 1, sets how fast the weights fade. In the animation: Top row: the rewards ahead. Each lane looks a different number of steps ahead, teal, then adds a guess, purple. Gold bars show how much each lane counts. lambda slides between short and long.

gae:6.t: Turning the knob. lambda = 0 means trust the critic after one step. lambda = 1 means use the full real return. Values in between give a smooth middle ground. In the animation: Left: how much weight each n-step return gets for the current lambda. Short ones are purple, long ones teal. Right: where the resulting estimates land compared with the true value at the gold centre. Try it: Drag lambda from 0 to 1 and watch the dots tighten or spread. For example: Like advice: trust your own eyes for the next few steps, and a forecast for the far future.

gae:7.t: In practice. G A E was introduced by John Schulman and colleagues in 2015. lambda = 0.95 is the near-universal default in P P O, and it’s one reason P P O trains so reliably.

gae:8.t: In a nutshell. n-step: n real rewards, then the critic. Small n biased, large n noisy. G A E blends every n with one knob lambda. Default lambda about 0.95 in P P O.

ppo:0.t: P P O. Improve the policy, but not too much at once.

ppo:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy: the agent’s rule for picking an action in each situation. Update: one round of changing the network’s numbers to improve it. Batch: a chunk of collected experience used for training together. Ratio: new probability of an action divided by its old probability.

ppo:2.t: The danger. Policy gradient steps are noisy. One too-big update can wreck a good policy. Worse, the broken policy then collects bad data, so it can be hard to ever recover. In the animation: The teal curve is how well the policy plays at each setting, with a cliff just past the peak. Gold hops are update steps. Small steps climb safely; too big a step jumps off the cliff and gets stuck. Try it: Push the step size up until the agent jumps off the cliff.

ppo:3.t: The idea. Improve the policy, but keep each new version close to the old one. Small, safe steps, many times. That’s Proximal Policy Optimization: proximal means nearby.

ppo:4.t: Clip the ratio. For each action, compare its new probability with the old one: the ratio. If it drifts beyond a band, typically 0.8 to 1.2, P P O stops pushing further in that direction. In the animation: The horizontal axis is how much the new policy changed an action’s probability. The teal line is P P O’s objective. The gold dot is pushed along it until it hits the flat part, the clip, where pushing stops. For example: An action had 10% chance. P P O will happily move it to 12%, but gets no extra credit for 30%.

ppo:5.t: Reuse data safely. Because of the clip, P P O can take several passes over the same batch of experience without going off the rails. That squeezes more learning out of each game played. In the animation: The same experience is reused for several passes. Without clipping, the good action’s chance keeps inflating, in red. P P O, in teal, stops once it leaves the gold band around the old chance. Try it: Change epsilon: the teal bar may only move inside the gold band.

ppo:6.t: Its ancestor, TRPO. Trust Region Policy Optimization, from 2015, enforced the same small-step rule with heavier maths. P P O, from 2017, gets most of the benefit with a much simpler trick.

ppo:7.t: Everywhere. P P O became the default for game agents, simulated robots, and the reinforcement step of R L H F for chatbots. OpenAI Five, which beat world champions at Dota 2, was trained with P P O.

ppo:8.t: In a nutshell. Big policy updates can wreck performance. Keep the new policy close to the old. Clipped probability ratio does it simply. Default for games, robots and R L H F.

sac:0.t: Entropy & Soft Actor-Critic. Reward the agent for keeping its options open.

sac:1.t: Words you’ll need. Entropy: a measure of how random or spread out choices are. Off-policy: able to learn from old experience, even from a different behaviour. Critic: a learned guess of how much reward lies ahead. Continuous control: tasks where actions are smooth numbers, like motor torques.

sac:2.t: Entropy. Entropy measures how spread out a policy’s choices are. Always picking the same action means low entropy. Spreading bets across many actions means high entropy. In the animation: Six bars are the probabilities of six actions. As temperature rises, the bars even out and the purple entropy meter fills, meaning more exploring. When it falls, one bar dominates. For example: A fair die has high entropy. A die that always lands on six has zero.

sac:3.t: A new goal. Maximum-entropy R L asks the agent to collect reward and stay as random as it can while doing so. Score = reward + alpha (alpha) times entropy. Alpha sets how much randomness is worth. In the animation: Five routes with different values, Q. Bars show how often the agent picks each; pink dots are recent picks. Alpha sets how much spreading out is rewarded; the purple meter shows the entropy. Try it: Drag alpha: small means greedy, large means spread out.

sac:4.t: Why that helps. Built-in exploration: the agent keeps trying alternatives. It also avoids collapsing early onto one mediocre trick, and copes better when the world nudges it off course.

sac:5.t: An analogy. Learning several routes to work, not just one. You still take a fast route, but when a road is closed you already know a backup. In the animation: Two drivers, home to office. Thick lines are routes a driver knows well. Both use the fast top route, until it closes. The greedy driver has no backup; the max-entropy driver already knows the others.

sac:6.t: Soft Actor-Critic. sack puts this into an actor-critic. It learns off-policy from a memory of old experience, uses two critics and trusts the lower one, and tunes alpha automatically.

sac:7.t: Where it shines. sack, from Tuomas Haarnoja and colleagues in 2018, is a go-to for continuous control. It taught a real four-legged robot to walk from about two hours of real experience.

sac:8.t: In a nutshell. Entropy = how random the policy is. Goal: reward plus alpha times entropy. Built-in exploration and robustness. sack: stable off-policy continuous control.

ddpg:0.t: Continuous Control: D D P G & T D 3. D Q N for steering wheels and robot joints.

ddpg:1.t: Words you’ll need. Continuous action: an action that is any number in a range, like 0.37. Q-value: a guess of the total future reward for an action in a situation. Replay buffer: a memory of past experience the agent learns from again. Target network: a slowly updated copy of a network, used for steady learning targets.

ddpg:2.t: The problem. D Q N picks the action with the highest Q-value by checking every option. With a steering wheel there are infinitely many angles, so checking each one is impossible.

ddpg:3.t: Learn the best action. Train an actor network that outputs a single action directly. It learns by asking the critic: which small change to my action would raise the Q-value? Then it moves that way. In the animation: The teal curve is the critic’s score for every possible action, like a steering angle. The pink dot is the actor’s action, sliding uphill along the curve. Gold dots are small exploration jitters.

ddpg:4.t: Like climbing a hill. Picture the critic’s Q-values as a hilly landscape over all possible actions. The actor is a hiker always stepping uphill, toward the best action for each situation. In the animation: The teal curve is the critic’s score for every steering angle. The robot is the actor’s current choice; the gold arrow shows which way is uphill. It keeps stepping until it reaches a peak. Try it: Tap anywhere along the curve to drop the actor there. For example: Steering 0.30 scores 5, steering 0.32 scores 5.4. The actor shifts toward 0.32.

ddpg:5.t: D D P G. Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, from 2015, combined this with D Q N’s tricks: a replay buffer, target networks, and random noise added to actions so it keeps exploring.

ddpg:6.t: T D 3 fixes it. D D P G overestimated Q-values and was fragile. T D 3, from 2018, keeps two critics and trusts the lower, updates the actor less often, and smooths its targets. Much more reliable. In the animation: The dashed line is each action’s true value. Pink and purple are two critics, each with its own false spike. The thick teal curve takes the lower of the two everywhere, so the spikes cancel.
