ddpg:7.t: Where it’s used. Classic benchmarks are simulated robots like HalfCheetah and Hopper in MuJoCo, plus robot arms. T D 3 and sack are the usual starting points for these tasks today.

ddpg:8.t: In a nutshell. Can’t check every continuous action. Actor climbs the critic’s Q landscape. Reuses replay and target networks. T D 3 adds twin critics and delays.

modelbased:0.t: Model-Based R L. Learn how the world works, then plan in your head.

modelbased:1.t: Words you’ll need. Model: a predictor of what happens next if you take an action. Planning: trying out actions in your head before doing them for real. Rollout: a chain of imagined steps, one after another. Sample efficiency: how much a method learns from each bit of real experience.

modelbased:2.t: Two ways to learn. Model-free agents learn purely by trial and error. Model-based agents also learn how the world works, then use that knowledge to think ahead.

modelbased:3.t: What a model is. A model predicts the next state and reward for a given state and action. Sometimes it’s given, like the rules of chess. Often it has to be learned from data. In the animation: The robot wanders the grid. After each move it notes where it was, which way it went, where it landed and the reward. That notebook on the right is its model; purple arrows mark known moves. For example: A thermostat model: heater on for 10 minutes, room goes from 18 to 20 degrees.

modelbased:4.t: Plan before acting. With a model you can imagine: if I do this, then that, where do I end up? Try many options in your head, then do the most promising one for real. In the animation: The robot pauses and imagines each possible move with its model, the dashed purple arrows, with a predicted score. The best, in gold, is then taken for real.

modelbased:5.t: Why it’s attractive. Imagined experience is free. Real experience with robots, patients or expensive machines is slow and costly. A good model can cut the real data needed dramatically.

modelbased:6.t: An old idea. Richard Sutton’s Dyna, from 1990, learned a model and mixed real updates with imagined ones. The same spirit runs through modern systems like MuZero and Dreamer.

modelbased:7.t: The pitfall. Small model errors snowball over long imagined rollouts. Worse, a planner will happily exploit any mistake that promises fake reward. Short rollouts and uncertainty estimates help. In the animation: A thrown ball. Teal is its real path; purple dashes are the path the model imagines, one step at a time. A small error each step adds up, so the red gap grows the further ahead it imagines. Try it: Set the error to 0, then raise it, and watch the red gap. For example: A sat-nav with one wrong road confidently routes you into a lake.

modelbased:8.t: In a nutshell. A model predicts next state and reward. Plan by imagining before acting. Saves costly real experience. Model errors compound and get exploited.

mcts:0.t: Monte Carlo Tree Search. Grow a search tree toward the most promising moves.

mcts:1.t: Words you’ll need. Search tree: a map of possible moves, then replies, then replies to those. Node: one position in the tree. Playout: a quick game played to the end, often with random moves. U C B: a rule that favours good-looking or rarely tried options.

mcts:2.t: The problem. In Go there are about 250 legal moves per turn. Looking even a few moves ahead creates more positions than you could ever check. You need to search selectively.

mcts:3.t: Four steps, repeated. Select: walk down the tree using U C B. Expand: add a new position. Simulate: play it out quickly. Back up: send the result back up the path. In the animation: A search tree grows. Each round follows promising gold branches, adds a new node, plays a quick random game in purple, then sends the result back up in green. Numbers count visits.

mcts:4.t: A tiny example. Move A has won 6 of 10 playouts, move B 1 of 2. U C B might still try B, because 2 tries is too few to judge. Each loop, the counts update and the tree grows. In the animation: Three candidate moves with their wins out of playouts. Each bar is the move’s U C B score: teal win rate plus a gold bonus that is big when a move has few tries. The tallest bar gets the next playout. Try it: Tap to run playouts and see which move U C B picks next.

mcts:5.t: Lopsided on purpose. The tree grows deep where moves look good and stays shallow elsewhere. Effort goes where it matters, instead of searching everything equally. In the animation: Watch where the tree grows: most new nodes, and the highest visit counts, pile up under the branch that keeps winning, while weak branches stay short. For example: Like a detective spending most time on the most promising leads.

mcts:6.t: Stop anytime. M C T S is anytime: halt whenever time runs out and play the move that was visited most at the top of the tree. More thinking time simply gives better moves.

mcts:7.t: Where it shines. M C T S took off around 2006 and transformed computer Go. It sits at the heart of AlphaGo, which beat Lee Sedol in 2016, and is used in puzzle solving and planning.

mcts:8.t: In a nutshell. Select, expand, simulate, back up. Focuses effort on promising moves. Anytime: more thinking, better moves. The search engine behind AlphaGo.

alphazero:0.t: AlphaZero. Self-play + tree search + one neural network.

alphazero:1.t: Words you’ll need. Self-play: an agent learning by playing games against copies of itself. M C T S: a search that grows a tree of moves toward promising ones. Policy head: the part of the network that suggests likely good moves. Value head: the part of the network that guesses who is winning.

alphazero:2.t: Starting from zero. AlphaZero is given only the rules of the game. No human games, no opening books, no expert tips. Everything it knows, it learns by playing against itself.

alphazero:3.t: The loop. Play many games against itself using tree search. Train the network on those games. Use the improved network to play the next batch. Repeat. In the animation: A cycle of four stages: play against itself, store the games, train the network, and use the network to guide the search. The gold dot goes round, and each lap is one generation.

alphazero:4.t: One network, two heads. A single network looks at a position and outputs two things. The policy head suggests which moves are worth searching. The value head estimates who is likely to win. In the animation: A tic-tac-toe position goes into one network. The top output lights up the squares worth searching, the policy head. The bottom output, the value head, estimates X’s chance of winning.

alphazero:5.t: Search as a teacher. Tree search guided by the network finds better moves than the network alone. The network is then trained to imitate those search results, so each round it gets stronger. In the animation: Purple bars are the network’s first guess for five moves. Gold bars show where the tree search spent its playouts. Then the network is trained so its purple bars match the gold. For example: A student checks answers with careful working, then learns to get them right at a glance.

alphazero:6.t: Results. DeepMind’s AlphaZero, in 2017, reached superhuman play at chess, shogi and Go. In chess it overtook the top engine Stockfish after only hours of self-play training.

alphazero:7.t: What came next. MuZero, from 2019, went further: it isn’t even told the rules. It learns its own model of the game and plans with it, and also mastered Atari games.

alphazero:8.t: In a nutshell. Learns from the rules alone, via self-play. Network guides search, search trains network. Superhuman at chess, shogi and Go. MuZero learned the rules too.

worldmodels:0.t: World Models & Dreamer. Learn to dream the game, then practise inside the dream.

worldmodels:1.t: Words you’ll need. Model: the agent’s own learned guess of what the world does next. Latent state: a short list of numbers that summarises what the agent sees. Rollout: playing out a sequence of steps, one after another. Policy: the agent’s rule for picking an action in each situation.

worldmodels:2.t: The problem. Real experience is expensive. A robot needs hours, a game needs millions of frames. What if the agent could practise in its head instead? For example: A pilot trains in a flight simulator before flying a real plane.

worldmodels:3.t: Dream a little. A world model is a learned simulator. It watches real play and learns to predict what happens next after each action.

worldmodels:4.t: Squeeze the picture. Predicting every pixel is wasteful. So the model first compresses each image into a small latent state, then learns how that summary changes. In the animation: First the agent watches the real ball and squeezes what it sees into a small code, the purple bars. Then it closes its eyes and practises in a dream the model generates, in purple.

worldmodels:5.t: Practise in imagination. The policy is then trained on imagined rollouts: thousands of dreamed futures inside the model, which cost almost nothing to run. In the animation: Left: the real world, where each step is slow. Right: the dream. From the gold dot (now), the model imagines many possible futures, drawn as purple lines, and the policy practises on all of them. For example: Collect 1 hour of real play, then dream 100 hours of practice from it.

worldmodels:6.t: Why the summary works. You only need to predict what matters for reward. The details that never change the outcome can be thrown away. For example: You can imagine catching a ball without picturing every blade of grass.

worldmodels:7.t: Famous examples. World Models (2018) learned car racing inside its own dream. DreamerV3 (2023) used one set of settings across many tasks and collected diamonds in Minecraft from scratch.

worldmodels:8.t: The catch. If the dream is wrong, the agent learns tricks that only work in the dream. So these methods keep checking the model against fresh real experience. In the animation: The teal line is what really happens; the dashed pink line is what the world model imagines. A tiny mistake each step adds up, so the red gap grows the further ahead it dreams. Try it: Drag the error slider: even small errors grow far ahead.

worldmodels:9.t: In a nutshell. A world model is a learned simulator. It works on a compact latent summary. Train the policy on imagined rollouts. Watch out for flaws in the dream.

shaping:0.t: Reward Shaping. Add hints so the agent isn’t searching in the dark.

shaping:1.t: Words you’ll need. Reward: a number the agent gets after each step; higher is better. Sparse reward: a reward that almost never shows up, often only at the very end. Optimal policy: the best possible way of behaving for a task.

shaping:2.t: The problem. If the only reward comes at the very end, a beginner moving at random may never stumble onto it, so it never learns anything. For example: A maze with one exit 200 steps away: random wandering almost never finds it.

shaping:3.t: Give hints. Reward shaping adds small extra rewards along the way that point in the right direction, like a game of hot and cold. In the animation: Two copies of the same maze. Left: reward only at the flag, so the pink dot wanders randomly. Right: squares get warmer closer to the goal, and the dot heads straight there.

shaping:4.t: A worked example. Give plus 0.1 for every step that moves closer to the exit and minus 0.1 for every step away. Now even early wandering gets useful feedback. In the animation: The pink dot wanders on a grid. Each time it gets closer to the flag it gets a small green +0.1, and each step away a red minus 0.1: a hot-and-cold game.

shaping:5.t: The danger. Bad hints change what the agent is really chasing. It may farm the hints and ignore the real goal. In the animation: The pink agent should walk to the flag. Each gold hint coin pays a little and comes back after a moment. Once a coin exists, the agent circles it forever instead of finishing. Try it: Tap cells to add or remove hint coins and watch it give up on the flag. For example: Reward a robot for touching the ball, and it may learn to vibrate against the ball forever instead of scoring.

shaping:6.t: The safe recipe. Give each state a potential, a score like minus the distance to the goal. The bonus for a step is the new potential minus the old one. Loops then earn nothing overall.

shaping:7.t: Why it is safe. Ng, Harada and Russell showed in 1999 that this potential-based kind of shaping speeds learning without changing which policy is optimal.

shaping:8.t: In a nutshell. Sparse rewards make learning slow. Shaping adds guiding hints. Careless hints get farmed. Potential-based shaping keeps the best policy.

hacking:0.t: Reward Hacking. You get what you reward, not what you meant.

hacking:1.t: Words you’ll need. Reward function: the rule, written by a person, that hands out points. Loophole: a way to score points the designer never intended. Reward model: a learned program that guesses how good an answer is.

hacking:2.t: The problem. A reward is only a stand-in for what we want. An agent optimises the number, not our intention, and it is very good at finding gaps.

hacking:3.t: Specification gaming. When the agent finds a loophole that scores high while ignoring the designer’s intent, we call it reward hacking or specification gaming. In the animation: A boat race. The reward is points for hitting targets, so the boat circles the same three targets forever, scoring more and more, and never reaches the finish line.

hacking:4.t: The boat race. In the game CoastRunners, an agent learned to spin in circles hitting respawning targets. It scored more than finishing the race, while catching fire. In the animation: The speedboat races around the track as intended. The pink boat found three gold targets that keep coming back, and circles them forever. It scores more points without ever finishing a lap.

hacking:5.t: More examples. Simulated robots exploited physics bugs to slide instead of walk. A Tetris-playing program learned to pause the game forever so it would never lose.

hacking:6.t: An old law. Goodhart’s law says that when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Reward hacking is Goodhart’s law for machines. In the animation: The gold line is the score the agent optimises; the teal line is what we really want. With a little optimisation both rise. Push harder and the score keeps climbing while the real goal falls. Try it: Push the slider right: the score climbs while the real goal falls. For example: Pay a team per bug fixed, and some people start writing bugs to fix.

hacking:7.t: Why it matters today. Chatbots trained with a reward model can learn to please the reward model, sounding confident or flattering instead of being correct.

hacking:8.t: Defences. Test in varied situations, watch what the agent actually does, keep it close to sensible behaviour, and patch the reward when you find a loophole.

hacking:9.t: In a nutshell. Agents optimise the number, not the intent. Classic: boat circling for points. Goodhart’s law for machines. A core worry in AI safety.

curiosity:0.t: Curiosity & Intrinsic Motivation. Reward the agent for being surprised.

curiosity:1.t: Words you’ll need. Exploration: trying new things to find out what works. Intrinsic reward: a bonus the agent gives itself, not one from the task. Prediction error: how wrong a guess about the next moment turned out to be.

curiosity:2.t: The problem. Some tasks give almost no reward until you have done many things right. Random button mashing will not get you there. For example: In a big game, the first point might need 100 correct moves in a row.

curiosity:3.t: Be curious. Children explore because new things are fun. Intrinsic motivation gives the agent that drive: a bonus for reaching new or surprising places. In the animation: The gold dot explores a grid with no outside reward. Bright purple squares are new and surprising, so visiting them feels rewarding. Once seen, they fade, so it moves on to unseen ones.

curiosity:4.t: Counting visits. The simplest bonus: the fewer times you have visited a place, the bigger the reward for going there. Familiar places become boring. In the animation: Each cell shows how often the pink agent has been there. Gold sparkle cells are unvisited and pay the biggest bonus, so the agent keeps heading for them and slowly covers the whole map.

curiosity:5.t: Measuring surprise. A second way: train a small model to predict what comes next. Where its prediction error is high, the place is unfamiliar, so pay a bonus there. For example: Error of 0.9 in a new room earns a big bonus; 0.05 in the start room earns almost none.

curiosity:6.t: A famous win. Montezuma’s Revenge is an Atari game with very rare rewards. In 2018, a curiosity method called Random Network Distillation beat the average human score.

curiosity:7.t: The noisy TV. A screen of random static is endlessly surprising. A naive curious agent will stare at it forever and never do the task. In the animation: The room has five areas; the bars show how surprising each still is. Visiting an area makes it boring. The TV shows random static, which stays surprising forever, so the curious pink agent gets stuck there. Try it: Tap the TV to switch it off and set the agent free. For example: Fix: only reward surprise about things the agent can actually learn to predict.

curiosity:8.t: In a nutshell. Bonus reward for novelty or surprise. Use visit counts or prediction error. Cracked very sparse games. Beware the noisy TV.

imitation:0.t: Imitation Learning. Skip the reward: just copy an expert.

imitation:1.t: Words you’ll need. Demonstration: a recording of an expert doing the task. Supervised learning: learning from examples that come with the right answer. Policy: the agent’s rule for picking an action in each situation.

imitation:2.t: The problem. Writing a good reward is hard, and trial and error can be slow or dangerous. But we often have experts who can simply show the task. For example: It’s easier to drive a car than to write down a score for “good driving”.

imitation:3.t: Behaviour cloning. Record the expert, then turn each moment into an example: this situation, the expert did that. Train the policy to give the same answer.

imitation:4.t: The trap. The copy makes a small mistake and drifts somewhere the expert never went. There it has no examples, so it errs more, and the errors pile up. In the animation: The gold dashed line is the expert’s road. First, the pink car copies demos and slowly drifts off the road. Then with dagger, the expert corrects it where it actually goes, the green arrows, and it stays on.

imitation:5.t: A walked example. A car drifts 30 centimetres off the lane centre. The expert never drove there, so the learner has no idea how to recover, and drifts further. In the animation: The teal band is where the expert drove, the only places with examples. The pink line is the copied driver. Inside the band it corrects itself; once a slip takes it outside, it has no examples and drifts off the road. Try it: Raise the slip size and watch small slips turn into crashes.

imitation:6.t: The dagger fix. Let the learner drive, then ask the expert: what would you have done here? Add those answers to the data and retrain. dagger was introduced in 2011. In the animation: Each round, the learner drives and the expert adds gold arrows saying what to do where it ended up. The gold band of known situations grows, and the pink line stays on the road.

imitation:7.t: Where it’s used. Robots learning from people steering them remotely, self-driving prototypes, and the pre-training of chatbots, which imitate human text. For example: NVIDIA’s 2016 car learned to steer from about 72 hours of human driving.

imitation:8.t: In a nutshell. Learn by copying expert demonstrations. Small errors compound in unseen places. dagger asks the expert about those places. Common in robots, cars and chatbots.

irl:0.t: Inverse R L. Watch the expert, figure out what they want.

irl:1.t: Words you’ll need. Reward: a number the agent gets after each step; higher is better. Demonstration: a recording of an expert doing the task. Trajectory: the path of situations and actions in one run.

irl:2.t: Flip the problem. Normal R L goes from reward to behaviour. Inverse R L goes the other way: from behaviour, work out the reward that explains it. In the animation: Pink lines are expert demos arriving one by one. Squares light up where experts head, near the end of their routes. The brightest square, marked with a star, is the guessed goal.

irl:3.t: An analogy. You watch a friend always take the longer road home. You guess they care about avoiding traffic more than distance. That guess is a reward. In the animation: The pink dot is a friend driving from home to work. They always take the long empty road rather than the short jammed one. With each trip, our guess of their reward shifts: they hate traffic more than they mind time.

irl:4.t: Why not just copy?. A reward is a short, reusable description of the goal. In a new city with new roads, you can plan with the reward instead of copying old routes.

irl:5.t: The ambiguity. Many rewards explain the same behaviour. Even “every action is worth zero” technically fits. So methods need a rule for picking a sensible answer. In the animation: The pink arrows are what the expert did. The grid colours show a guessed reward. Three very different guesses, even "everything is zero", all explain the same path.

irl:6.t: Maximum entropy. A popular rule, from 2008: choose the reward that explains the expert while assuming nothing extra. Behaviour that fits equally well gets equal belief. For example: Two routes take the same time? Assume the driver likes both equally.

irl:7.t: Uses and cousins. Used to learn drivers’ trade-offs between speed, comfort and safety from their trajectories. gale (2016) imitates without writing the reward down at all.

irl:8.t: In a nutshell. Infer the reward from demonstrations. A reward transfers to new situations. Many rewards fit, so pick a sensible one. Max-entropy I R L and gale are classics.

offline:0.t: Offline R L. Learn from a fixed log of data, with no new trials.

offline:1.t: Words you’ll need. Dataset: a fixed collection of past situations, actions and rewards. Value: how much total reward the agent expects from a choice. Exploration: trying new things to find out what works.

offline:2.t: The setting. You get a dataset that someone else collected. You must learn a good policy from it, and you may not try anything new. For example: Hospital records, past robot runs, or logs of which recommendations people clicked.

offline:3.t: Why bother?. In many places trial and error is unsafe or expensive. You cannot test random treatments on patients, but you do have years of records.

offline:4.t: Why it is hard. The learner may believe an action it has never seen is amazing. Normally it would try it and find out. Offline, nothing ever corrects the mistake. In the animation: White dots are the logged data: states across, actions up. The red cross is a naive agent chasing a high value where there’s no data. The teal dot stays close to the data, which is safer.

offline:5.t: A walked example. The log shows doses of 1 and 2 units only. The learner’s guess for 5 units is pure invention, say a value of 100, so it picks 5. Disaster. In the animation: Teal dots are the logged doses, only 1 and 2 units. The pink line is the learner’s guess of how good each dose is; the dashed line is the truth. Far from the data, the guess is made up and wildly optimistic. Try it: Slide the dose outside the data and compare guess with reality.

offline:6.t: Stay close to the data. Offline methods are conservative: they lower the value of actions the data does not cover, or simply stick to actions the data contains. In the animation: The gold line is a cautious guess: values far from the logged data are pushed down. The gold star is the dose it would pick. More caution pulls the choice back to where there is evidence. Try it: Drag caution to zero: the star runs off to an untested dose. For example: C Q L pushes down values of unseen actions; I Q L only learns from actions in the log.

offline:7.t: Where it’s heading. Offline R L lets us reuse the huge logs that already exist, and often serves as a warm start before a small amount of careful real-world practice.

offline:8.t: In a nutshell. Learn only from a fixed dataset. Danger: overrating unseen actions. Conservative methods stay near the data. Great where trial and error is unsafe.

rlhf:0.t: R L H F. How chatbots are tuned with human preferences.

rlhf:1.t: Words you’ll need. Language model: a program that writes text by predicting the next word. Reward model: a learned program that guesses how good an answer is. P P O: a popular, stable method for improving a policy with rewards. Fine-tuning: extra training that adjusts an already trained model.

rlhf:2.t: The problem. What score does a helpful, honest answer deserve? Nobody can write that rule as code. But people can easily say which of two answers is better.

rlhf:3.t: Step 1: ask people. Show people two answers to the same question and ask which they prefer. Collect many thousands of these comparisons. In the animation: Two answers to the same question. Each time someone picks the better one, the reward model below updates its scores: answer styles that win go up, styles that lose go down. Try it: Tap the answer you prefer and watch the scores change. For example: Answer A explains clearly, answer B rambles. Most people pick A.

rlhf:4.t: Step 2: a reward model. Train a reward model to predict which answer people would pick. Now we have an automatic judge that scores any answer. In the animation: Two answers to one prompt. A person picks the better one, ticked green. That choice trains the reward model, gold. The reward model then scores the language model, which learns to score higher.

rlhf:5.t: Step 3: practise. Use R L, often P P O, to fine-tune the language model so its answers get higher scores from the reward model.

rlhf:6.t: Don’t drift too far. A penalty grows as the model moves away from its starting version. This stops it exploiting quirks of the reward model with weird text. In the animation: Bars show how often the model gives each style of answer. The reward model wrongly loves flattering, long answers. With a weak penalty the tuned model piles onto that style: the judge’s score rises while real quality drops. Try it: Lower the penalty and see real quality drop.

rlhf:7.t: Famous result. InstructGPT (2022): people preferred answers from a model tuned this way over a plain model more than 100 times bigger.

rlhf:8.t: Newer variants. D P O skips the separate R L step and learns from the comparisons directly. Other methods replace human judges with AI feedback or written principles.

rlhf:9.t: In a nutshell. People compare pairs of answers. A reward model learns their taste. R L tunes the chatbot to score well. A penalty stops drifting and hacking.

pomdp:0.t: Partial Observability (P O M D P). What to do when you can’t see the whole picture.

pomdp:1.t: Words you’ll need. State: a full description of the situation right now. Observation: the part of the situation the agent can actually see. Belief: the agent’s best guess, as chances, of what the true state is.

pomdp:2.t: The problem. Basic R L assumes the agent sees the full state. Real agents only get observations: clues from sensors or cameras that hide part of the story. In the animation: The pink agent only sees the cells right around it. Dim cells are places it remembers, and question marks are still unknown. The gem is hidden somewhere, so it has to explore and remember. Try it: Tap a cell to send the agent exploring through the fog. For example: A robot’s camera can’t see behind a wall.

pomdp:3.t: A name for it. This setting is called a P O M D P: a partially observable Markov decision process. The world has a true state; the agent only glimpses it.

pomdp:4.t: Keep a belief. The agent keeps a belief: chances for each possible state. Every action and new observation updates those chances. In the animation: A corridor with three doors. The robot can’t see where it is. Its guess is the bars. Moving blurs the guess, and seeing a door or a wall sharpens it toward matching spots.

pomdp:5.t: A walked example. A robot is in one of two identical corridors, 50 to 50. It spots a red door that only corridor B has. Now it believes B with about 95 percent. In the animation: Two corridors look identical; the robot is really in B but cannot tell. The bar at the bottom is its belief: 50/50 until it sees the red door that only B has.

pomdp:6.t: Memory helps. Deep R L agents often get memory, through recurrent networks or transformers, so they can piece clues together over time. For example: Poker: you can’t see opponents’ cards, so you remember how they have been betting.

pomdp:7.t: Act to find out. Sometimes the best action earns nothing directly but gathers information, so later choices are better. For example: Opening a door just to see what is behind it.

pomdp:8.t: In a nutshell. The agent sees observations, not the state. A belief is a guess with chances. Memory pieces clues together. Sometimes act just to learn more.

hrl:0.t: Hierarchical R L. Think in sub-goals, not individual muscle twitches.

hrl:1.t: Words you’ll need. Policy: the agent’s rule for picking an action in each situation. Sub-goal: a smaller target on the way to the main goal. Skill: a reusable routine, like “open a door”.

hrl:2.t: The problem. Long tasks need thousands of tiny actions. When the reward finally arrives, it is hard to tell which of those tiny steps deserve credit.

hrl:3.t: Think like a person. You don’t plan dinner one muscle twitch at a time. You think in big steps: go to the kitchen, cook, serve. Each big step hides many small ones.

hrl:4.t: Manager and worker. A high-level manager policy picks a sub-goal every so often. A low-level worker policy takes the small steps to reach it. In the animation: A maze with four rooms. The manager, gold, picks the next flag: door 1, door 2, then the trophy. The worker, the pink dot, takes the single steps to reach each flag.

hrl:5.t: A walked example. Manager: “reach the door”. Worker takes about 40 steps to get there. Manager then decides only 5 times for the whole task, instead of 200. In the animation: The manager only picks the next flag (gold box). The pink worker takes the small steps to reach it. Count them: 3 manager decisions versus 13 worker steps.

hrl:6.t: Options. An option is a reusable skill: a mini-policy with a rule for when it can start and when it stops. The agent picks options like ordinary actions. In the animation: Each coloured bar is a reusable skill: it starts, runs on its own for a while, then stops when its job is done. The arrows below are the tiny actions each skill takes. For example: Make coffee = walk to kitchen, then grind beans, then brew.

hrl:7.t: Still open. Hand-designed sub-goals work well. Getting agents to discover good skills on their own is still an active research problem.

hrl:8.t: In a nutshell. Break long tasks into sub-goals. Manager picks goals, worker acts. Options are reusable skills. Discovering skills is still open.

marl:0.t: Multi-Agent R L. When several learners share one world.

marl:1.t: Words you’ll need. Agent: a learner that makes its own choices. Non-stationary: changing over time, so old lessons stop being true. Self-play: training against copies of yourself.

marl:2.t: Many agents. Many worlds hold several learners. They can be teammates, opponents, or a mix of both. In the animation: Two agents, pink and teal, race for the same coins. Each one’s best move depends on what the other does, so from either agent’s view, the world keeps changing. For example: Teammates: robot football. Opponents: chess. A mix: city traffic or a market.

marl:3.t: The problem. Everyone else is learning too, so the world you face keeps changing. A trick that worked yesterday stops working once others adapt. It is non-stationary.

marl:4.t: A walked example. You learn the goalkeeper always dives left, so you shoot right. The keeper learns too and starts diving right. Your old lesson is now wrong. In the animation: The teal line is how often the striker shoots right; the pink line is how often the keeper dives right. Each keeps adapting to the other, so the lines chase each other instead of settling.

marl:5.t: Train together, act alone. A popular recipe: during training, let a coach see everyone’s information. At test time, each agent acts only on what it can see itself. In the animation: Blue circles show what each agent can see. During training, a coach (gold) collects everyone’s information to give better feedback. At test time the coach is gone and each agent decides from its own view.

marl:6.t: Self-play. In competitive games, an agent can train against copies of itself. As it improves, so does its opponent, giving a steady stream of good practice.

marl:7.t: Highlights. OpenAI Five beat the Dota 2 world champions in 2019. AlphaStar reached Grandmaster level in StarCraft II. In hide-and-seek, agents invented tool use.

marl:8.t: In a nutshell. Several agents learning in one world. Others adapting makes the world change. Train together, act alone. Self-play gives endless opponents.

sim2real:0.t: Sim-to-Real & Domain Randomisation. Train in simulation, then deploy on a real robot.

sim2real:1.t: Words you’ll need. Simulator: a computer program that imitates the physical world. Reality gap: the differences between the simulator and the real world. Policy: the robot’s rule for choosing what to do.

sim2real:2.t: Why simulate?. Real robots are slow, they break, and you can’t run a thousand of them at once. A simulator runs thousands of copies, faster than real time, for free.

sim2real:3.t: The reality gap. Simulated friction, weight and lighting never match reality exactly. A policy that is perfect in the simulator can stumble on the real robot. In the animation: Top: in the simulator, a puck pushed with the learned force stops on the target. Bottom: the same push on a real floor with different friction overshoots or stops short. Try it: Set the real friction to 0.30 to match the simulator. For example: A robot that learned on a perfectly smooth simulated floor slips on a real rug.

sim2real:4.t: Randomise everything. Domain randomisation: during training, keep changing friction, masses, colours, lighting and delays at random. In the animation: A robot arm pushes a block in a series of simulators, each with random colours, friction, weight and lighting. Every sixth scene is the grey real world, which looks like just one more variation.

sim2real:5.t: Why that works. After seeing thousands of slightly different worlds, the policy must handle all of them. The real world then looks like just one more variation. In the animation: The blue band is the range of friction the policy saw during training; the white dots are random training worlds. Each below is a real-world test. Widen the band and more real worlds fall inside. Try it: Widen the randomisation until every real-world test passes. For example: Train with friction anywhere from 0.5 to 1.5, and the real 0.9 is easy.

sim2real:6.t: A famous example. In 2019, OpenAI’s robot hand solved a Rubik’s cube after training only in heavily randomised simulation.

sim2real:7.t: Walking robots. Four-legged robots, such as ANYmal, learned to walk over rough ground in simulation and then did it outdoors, on real hills and snow.

sim2real:8.t: In a nutshell. Simulation is cheap and runs in parallel. The reality gap breaks naive transfer. Randomise the simulator during training. Reality becomes one more variation.
